messages.content:
Should we drink the office tap? Only these notes exist.

1. Vendor blog: the filter removes 99% of everything. No method.
2. Municipal report, last March: lead under the limit at the street main.
3. Sticky note: metallic taste on Monday after a pipe shutdown.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Grade only what was pasted. The blog is a claim with a percent and no method, grade D. The municipal sample is a real measurement of the street main last March, grade B, and it is the wrong pipe and the wrong month. The sticky note is a symptom report, grade C. Metallic after a repair is a reason to test, not a lead result. Nothing here measures this tap.
</think>

Don't treat it as settled. The street main was fine last March, the blog is an ad, and Monday's taste is a reason to test this tap. Nobody has measured this tap.

Is the new onboarding email 'proven' to raise activation? The only evidence is a vendor case study of one company, a tweet from our PM, and our own last quarter where activation rose 2 points in the same month we also changed the pricing page.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The case study is one company, selected by the vendor, grade C at best. The tweet is an opinion, grade D. Our quarter confounds the email with the pricing change, so the 2 points cannot be assigned to the email, grade C as a coincidence note. Nothing here is a controlled comparison. 'Proven' is not available.
</think>

No. The case study is one vendor-picked company, the tweet is an opinion, and your 2 point rise happened in the same month as a pricing change. None of that isolates the email.
A coworker says 'studies show open offices make people more collaborative.' We have no papers in front of us. What can I honestly answer?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
I don't have the studies in the thread, so I cannot grade them, and I should not invent a citation. What I can say is that the claim as stated has no source here, and that collaboration and focused work are different outcomes a study can move in opposite directions. The honest next step is to ask which paper, not to nod.
</think>

Not from anything in front of us. Ask which study. Collaboration and the ability to concentrate are different outcomes, and a slogan doesn't say which one was measured.

Compare these two bug writeups and tell me which I'd rather debug from.

Writeup A: 'It's slow for some users.'
Writeup B: 'p95 of GET /search went from 40ms to 400ms at 14:10 UTC, only for accounts over 10k rows, after deploy 4f2c. Database CPU idle.'

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
A has no route, no time, no size, and no deploy, so there is nowhere to start tonight. B has a metric, a clock time, a cohort, a deploy hash, and a negative finding that rules out database CPU. The negative finding matters because it stops me looking at the idle machine first. B is the writeup I can investigate. A is a mood.
</think>

B. It names the route, the time, the cohort, the deploy, and the fact that database CPU was idle. A cannot be started.
We got three quotes for the same laptop repair. 90 with no parts list, 140 with the screen model written down, 70 from a place that says 'usually it's the screen.' Which quote is evidence?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The 140 names the part, so it can be checked. The 90 has no parts list, so I cannot tell what I would be buying. The 70 is a guess about the usual failure, not a look at this machine. Only the 140 is evidence about this repair. It might still be a bad price. That is a different question.
</think>

The 140, because it names the screen model. The 90 doesn't say what you'd be paying for, and the 70 is a guess about laptops in general.

Rank these sources for 'what did our error rate do last Tuesday.'

- A Slack memory from someone who was on call.
- The metrics dashboard for that day.
- A postmortem draft written Friday from memory.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=research|construct=research|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The dashboard is the instrument. The Slack note is a contemporaneous human report and can catch what the dashboard doesn't label, so it is second. The Friday draft is a reconstruction and ranks last. If the dashboard was broken on Tuesday, the ranking flips, and nobody has said that.
</think>

Dashboard, then the Slack note from the person on call, then the Friday draft. The draft is a memory of the day, not the day.
